R.q:
The city plans to build a five-story parking garage on the empty lot at Elm and Third Streets. The project would add 420 spaces and cost $11 million, paid for by a bond measure on the November ballot. City planners call the garage "badly needed" and say it would serve visitors to the hospital, the library and the new courthouse. Voters should see this money pit for what it is: a gift to downtown developers at the expense of ordinary taxpayers. Construction would take about 18 months.

Which phrase from the passage most clearly reveals the author's bias?
o: call the garage "badly needed"
paid for by a bond measure
this money pit
the empty lot at Elm and Third Streets
R.w: "Money pit" is loaded language: a negative label that pushes readers to see the garage as wasteful before any evidence is weighed. That emotional slant reveals the author's bias against the project.

n.0: "Badly needed" is a judgment, but it belongs to the city planners, whom the author quotes. Reporting another group's view is not the author's own slant, and the planners' view is the opposite of the author's.
n.1: This states how the project would be financed, a neutral and checkable detail.
n.3: "Empty lot" describes the site's current condition and can be checked; it carries no judgment.

R.q:
Hurricane Delia tore across Port Ellis last weekend with winds of 120 miles per hour. It ripped the roofs from more than half of the town's homes, flooded the only bridge to the mainland and left 9,000 residents without power. At a press conference on Monday, Mayor Teresa Ruiz looked at the crowd of reporters and said, "We've had a bit of a rough week."

The mayor's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: understatement
allusion
hyperbole
personification
R.w: Calling a devastating hurricane "a bit of a rough week" makes the situation sound far less serious than it is. Deliberately downplaying something is understatement.

n.1: An allusion refers to a well-known person, place, event or work; the mayor refers to none.
n.2: Hyperbole is the opposite: exaggerating to make something seem bigger. The mayor makes the disaster sound smaller.
n.3: Personification gives human traits to a non-human thing; the mayor describes the town's week without giving any object human qualities.

R.q:
Marcus signed up to volunteer at Maple Court Senior Living because his school required twenty service hours. For the first few Thursdays, he read the newspaper aloud to Mr. Hale, who corrected his pronunciation and rarely smiled. Marcus counted the minutes. In October, Mr. Hale mentioned that he had once flown cargo planes in Alaska. Curious, Marcus asked a question, and then another. By December, Marcus had logged sixty hours, far more than he needed, and had filled a notebook with Mr. Hale's stories.

Which statement expresses a theme of the passage rather than its topic or plot?
o: A high school student's volunteer work at a senior living center
Marcus logs sixty hours after he begins asking Mr. Hale about Alaska.
Schools should require students to complete community service hours.
Curiosity about others can turn an obligation into a real connection.
R.w: A theme is a general message stated as a full sentence. Marcus's attitude changes when he becomes curious about Mr. Hale, turning required hours into a relationship he values.

n.0: This phrase names the topic; it states no message.
n.1: This retells events from the plot rather than stating a general message.
n.2: This is an opinion about school policy; the story never argues for requiring service hours.

R.q:
A dental hygiene student is writing a report on BrightWhite, a new whitening toothpaste. The company's website claims that the toothpaste is "safe for daily use on tooth enamel." The student wants to cite evidence on this question that her instructor will accept as trustworthy. Her instructor has told the class that a source's funding, expertise, and review process all affect how much weight its evidence deserves. She has found four possible sources.

Which source would provide the most credible evidence about the toothpaste's safety for enamel?
o: Online reviews from customers who used the toothpaste for a year
A video from a popular actress who says the product worked for her
A study designed, funded, and published by the toothpaste company
An independent lab study published in a peer-reviewed dental journal
R.w: An independent study that passed peer review has no stake in the product and was checked by other experts, so it is the most credible evidence on safety.

n.0: Customer reviews are anecdotal and cannot measure enamel damage.
n.1: An actress is not a dental expert; her endorsement is an appeal to false authority.
n.2: The company has a financial interest in a favorable result, a conflict of interest that lowers credibility.

R.q:
Read the description of the pictograph.

Title: Blood Donations Collected at the Campus Drive
Key: Each drop symbol = 20 pints. A half drop = 10 pints.
Monday: 4 drops
Tuesday: 2 and one-half drops
Wednesday: 5 drops
Thursday: 3 and one-half drops
Note: The drive was held in the student center from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. each day. Donors included students, faculty and staff, and a goal of 300 pints for the week was posted at the entrance.

According to the pictograph, how many more pints were collected on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
o: 2.5 pints
50 pints
25 pints
100 pints
R.w: Wednesday has 5 drops and Tuesday has 2.5 drops, a difference of 2.5 drops. Each drop is 20 pints, so 2.5 x 20 = 50 pints.

n.0: Counts the difference in symbols without converting drops to pints.
n.2: Uses 10 pints per drop, the value of a half drop, instead of 20.
n.3: 100 pints is Wednesday's total, not the difference between the two days.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Standing desks have become a common sight in offices, promoted as a cure for the health risks of sitting all day. Long periods of sitting are linked to back pain, weight gain and heart disease, so the appeal is easy to understand.

Standing all day, however, brings its own problems. Workers who stand for most of a shift report more leg swelling, foot pain and varicose veins than those who sit. A standing worker also burns only slightly more energy than a seated one, far too little to replace exercise.

Researchers who study workplace health now suggest a middle path: change positions often, take short walking breaks, and treat the desk as one tool among several rather than a solution in itself.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Standing desks are popular, but standing all day has its own costs, so experts advise shifting positions and moving often.
Standing burns only slightly more energy than sitting, so workers who use standing desks still need regular exercise.
Standing desks harm workers by causing leg swelling and foot pain, so offices should stop buying them for employees.
Sitting for long periods is linked to back pain, weight gain and heart disease, which explains why standing desks are popular.
R.w: The passage moves from the appeal of standing desks (paragraph 1), to the problems of standing all day (paragraph 2), to the recommended middle path (paragraph 3). This option keeps all three points in the same order and adds no opinion.

n.1: Too narrow: the energy comparison is one detail in the second paragraph.
n.2: Distortion with an added recommendation: the researchers suggest treating the desk as one tool among several, not that offices stop buying them.
n.3: Summarizes only the first paragraph and leaves out the problems with standing and the advice that follows.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The Ruiz Family Clinic opened in a converted storefront in 1994 with one doctor and two nurses. In 2001 it moved to a former bank building on Fourth Street, which gave it room for a small pharmacy. A dental wing followed in 2008, paid for by a state grant the clinic had first applied for in 2005. When the clinic celebrated its twenty-fifth anniversary in 2019, it employed 64 people, and plans were under way for a behavioral health center, which opened in 2022.

According to the passage, in what year did the clinic first have room for a pharmacy?
R.w: The passage says that the 2001 move to the former bank building gave the clinic room for a small pharmacy.

n.0: 1994 is when the clinic opened in a storefront; no pharmacy is mentioned then.
n.2: 2005 is when the clinic first applied for the grant that later paid for the dental wing.
n.3: 2008 is when the dental wing was added.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Teachers at Lincoln Middle School noticed that many students arrived tired and unfocused, and a survey found that about a third had eaten nothing before school. The cafeteria served a free breakfast, but it closed when the first bell rang, and students who came on late buses missed it.

Last fall the school tried a different approach. Carts of breakfast items were delivered to homerooms, and students ate during the first ten minutes of class while teachers took attendance. Within a month, the share of students eating school breakfast rose from 28 percent to 71 percent.

Some teachers had worried about spills and lost class time. After the first semester, most said the routine ran smoothly, and the school nurse reported fewer morning visits from students complaining of headaches or stomachaches.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: About a third of the students at Lincoln Middle School skipped breakfast at home, which left many of them tired and unfocused.
After many students skipped breakfast, the school began serving it in homerooms, which raised participation and mostly ran smoothly.
Breakfast participation at Lincoln Middle School rose from 28 percent to 71 percent within one month of the change.
Lincoln's homeroom breakfast raised students' focus and test scores, so nearby schools have begun to copy it.
R.w: A summary covers every paragraph in order: the problem (students skipping breakfast because the cafeteria closed at the bell), the solution (breakfast in homerooms) and the results (participation rose, worries mostly did not come true). Only this option includes all three.

n.0: Summarizes only the first paragraph; it leaves out the change the school made and its results.
n.2: Too narrow: the participation figures are one supporting detail from the second paragraph.
n.3: Goes beyond the passage: it never measures focus or test scores, and it never mentions other schools copying the plan.

R.q:
Grayson County Hospital began in 1912 as a six-bed clinic above a hardware store. In 1925, after a fire destroyed the store, the town raised money for a two-story brick building on Elm Street. During the 1950s, the hospital added a maternity ward and its first X-ray machine. A new emergency department opened in 1978, and in 2004 the hospital joined the regional Lakeshore Health network. Today, Grayson County Hospital has 140 beds and employs more than 900 people.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: compare and contrast
cause and effect
problem and solution
chronological order
R.w: The passage moves through the hospital's history date by date, from 1912 to today. Ordering events by time is chronological structure.

n.0: The passage traces one hospital over time; it does not set two subjects side by side.
n.1: One causal link appears (the fire led to a new building), but the passage as a whole is organized by dates, not by causes and their results.
n.2: No central problem is identified and solved; the passage lists milestones in order.

R.q:
Read the passage.

A city health report found that neighborhoods with more fast-food restaurants per block also had higher rates of diabetes. The same neighborhoods had fewer full-service grocery stores, lower average incomes and fewer parks than other parts of the city. The report's authors noted that their data showed only where these features occurred together, not which ones, if any, caused the others. They recommended a follow-up study that would track the same residents over several years.

Which statement is best supported by the report as described?
o: Residents of these neighborhoods prefer fast food to meals that they cook at home.
Closing fast-food restaurants would lower the city's rate of diabetes.
Diabetes is more common where several features cluster, but the cause is unclear.
Fast-food restaurants are the main cause of diabetes in these neighborhoods.
R.w: The report found that several features (fast food, fewer groceries, lower incomes, fewer parks) occur together with higher diabetes rates, and the authors state that the data do not show cause. This option keeps to that limit.

n.0: Unsupported: the report describes restaurant counts, not what residents prefer to eat.
n.1: A prediction that assumes fast food causes diabetes, which the data do not show.
n.3: Treats a correlation as a cause, which the authors explicitly warn against.

R.q:
Last year, the Oakmont Public Library stopped charging late fines on children's books. Over the next twelve months, the share of children's books returned within two weeks of the due date rose from 81 percent to 88 percent, and the number of new children's library cards rose by 12 percent. The library still charged fines on adult books, and that fine revenue stayed about the same. This month, the library board voted to end late fines on adult books as well, starting in January.

Which predictions are supported by the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Fine revenue from adult books will most likely drop after January.
Children's books will soon fall back to an 81 percent return rate.
Timely returns of adult books may improve after January, as they did for children's books.
The library will probably cut staff hours next year to make up for the lost fine revenue.
Adult books will most likely be returned late more often once their fines end.
R.w: Ending fines on children's books was followed by better returns, so a similar change for adult books may have a similar result. And once adult fines end, the adult fine revenue the library has been collecting will fall.

n.1: Nothing suggests the children's policy will change, so a reversal of the trend has no stated cause.
n.3: Staff cuts require an unstated event; the passage never mentions budgets or staffing.
n.4: The only evidence, from children's books, shows timely returns rising after fines ended; nothing points to more late returns.

R.q:
Read the timeline.

Measles in the United States: Selected Events
1912: Measles becomes a nationally reportable disease.
1954: The measles virus is first isolated in a laboratory.
1963: The first measles vaccine is licensed.
1968: An improved measles vaccine is licensed.
1971: The combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is licensed.
1989: A second dose of measles vaccine is recommended for children.
2000: Measles is declared eliminated from the United States.

According to the timeline, how many years passed between the licensing of the first measles vaccine and the declaration that measles had been eliminated from the United States?
o: 37 years
46 years
11 years
29 years
R.w: The first vaccine was licensed in 1963 and elimination was declared in 2000: 2000 - 1963 = 37 years.

n.1: Counts from 1954, when the virus was isolated, not when a vaccine was licensed.
n.2: Counts from 1989, when the second dose was recommended.
n.3: Counts from 1971, when the MMR vaccine was licensed, not the first measles vaccine.

R.q:
(1) Mercy Valley Hospital should turn the empty lot behind its east wing into a community garden. Patients could see green space from their windows, staff could take breaks outdoors, and the hospital's nutrition program could teach classes using fresh vegetables.

(2) Some board members argue that the lot should be saved for a future parking garage. However, the hospital's own ten-year plan places new parking on the west side of campus, and a garden could be moved in a single season if plans ever changed.

(3) A garden would cost less than $20,000 to build. The board should approve it this spring.

What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
o: to answer an objection to the author's proposal
to provide evidence that gardens improve patient health
to describe the location of the empty lot on the hospital campus
to summarize the costs and benefits of the garden
R.w: Paragraph 2 states an opposing view (save the lot for parking) and then rebuts it with the hospital's own plan and the garden's flexibility. Raising and answering an objection is a common purpose of a paragraph in a persuasive text.

n.1: Benefits to patients appear in paragraph 1, and no health evidence is offered anywhere in the passage.
n.2: The lot's location is given in paragraph 1; paragraph 2 mentions campus locations only to rebut the parking argument.
n.3: Cost appears only in paragraph 3, and paragraph 2 does not weigh costs against benefits.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Directions to the Westside Health Fair
From the Main Street bus stop, walk two blocks north to Elm Avenue and turn left. If the community center's front entrance is closed, go around to the side door on Birch Lane; otherwise, enter through the front. Once inside, check in at the welcome table. Visitors who preregistered online pick up a name badge; all other visitors fill out a paper form first. Free blood pressure checks are in Room 104, to the right of the welcome table, and flu shots are in Room 110, at the end of the hall.

Gloria did not preregister. When she arrives, the front entrance is open.

According to the directions, what should Gloria do immediately after entering?
o: Pick up her name badge at the welcome table
Go straight to Room 104 for a blood pressure check
Walk around to the side door on Birch Lane
Check in at the welcome table and fill out a paper form
R.w: The front entrance is open, so Gloria enters there. The next step for every visitor is to check in at the welcome table, and because she did not preregister, she fills out a paper form.

n.0: Badges are for visitors who preregistered online, and Gloria did not.
n.1: Skips the check-in step that every visitor completes first.
n.2: The side door is used when the front entrance is closed; Gloria found it open.

R.q:
Mara checked the supply cart twice before her shift began, then a third time after report. When the charge nurse asked why, Mara pointed to a note taped inside the top drawer. The reminder, written in her own handwriting, dated from the night a missing suction catheter had cost the team four minutes during an emergency. "I'd rather lose thirty seconds now," she said. The charge nurse nodded slowly. The following week, a cart check appeared on the start-of-shift list for every nurse on the unit.

Which conclusion about Mara is best supported by the passage?
o: She does not trust the other nurses on the unit to stock the supply cart correctly.
She was the nurse responsible for the missing catheter on the night of the emergency.
She was asked by the charge nurse to train the other nurses to check their carts.
A past delay she witnessed shapes the way she prepares for each of her shifts.
R.w: The note recalls the night a missing catheter cost four minutes, and Mara says she would rather lose thirty seconds now. Her repeated checks are explained by that earlier delay.

n.0: Nothing in the passage blames other nurses; her checks are tied to one past event, not to distrust of coworkers.
n.1: The note is in her handwriting, but the passage never says who left the catheter out; this is an assumption.
n.2: The charge nurse added a cart check to the shift list; the passage never says Mara was asked to train anyone.

R.q:
Read the memo.

MEMORANDUM
To: All Clinic Staff
From: Rafael Ortiz, Office Manager
Date: Monday, October 7
Re: Flu shot clinic for staff

Free flu shots for staff will be given in Conference Room B on Wednesday, October 16, from 7:00 to 9:00 a.m., and on Thursday, October 17, from 4:00 to 6:00 p.m. Sign up for a 10-minute slot on the sheet outside my office by Friday, October 11. Staff who received a flu shot elsewhere this season should email a copy of their record to Employee Health by October 31. Staff who cannot receive the vaccine for medical reasons must submit an exemption form, available from Employee Health, by the same date.

According to the memo, what is the deadline for signing up for a flu shot time slot?
o: Monday, October 7
Friday, October 11
Thursday, October 31
Wednesday, October 16
R.w: The memo says to sign up on the sheet outside the office manager's office by Friday, October 11.

n.0: October 7 is the date the memo was written.
n.2: October 31 is the deadline for outside vaccination records and exemption forms.
n.3: October 16 is the first day shots are given, not the sign-up deadline.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Five blocks sit in a row. From left to right they are red, blue, green, yellow and white. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the arrangement left by the step before it.
1. Swap the second and fourth blocks.
2. Move the block at the far left to the far right.
3. Place a black block between the green block and the blue block.
4. Remove the block that is second from the right.

What is the final order of the blocks, from left to right?
o: yellow, black, blue, white, red
white, red, yellow, green, blue
yellow, green, black, blue, white
yellow, green, black, blue, red
R.w: Step 1: red, yellow, green, blue, white. Step 2: yellow, green, blue, white, red. Step 3: yellow, green, black, blue, white, red. Step 4 removes the second block from the right (white): yellow, green, black, blue, red.

n.0: Removes the block second from the left (green) instead of second from the right.
n.1: Step 2 was reversed: the far-right block was moved to the far left.
n.2: Removes the block at the far right (red) instead of the one second from the right.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a high school teacher: This year our school began collecting phones at the front office each morning. Students pick them up at dismissal. Parents who need to reach their child during the day call the office, and we deliver the message within minutes. Since the change, I see students talking to each other at lunch, and fewer students drift off in class.

Passage 2
From a student: Taking our phones all day puts us at risk. If there is an emergency, or if my mom needs to tell me that my ride has changed, how is she supposed to reach me?

Based on Passage 1, how would its author most likely respond to the concern in Passage 2?
o: Families can still reach students through the school office.
Students should keep their phones on silent inside their bags.
Emergencies at school are too rare to plan for in a policy.
Students who need their phones may use them during lunch.
R.w: The teacher explains that parents call the office and messages are delivered within minutes. That arrangement directly answers the student's worry about being reached.

n.1: The teacher supports collecting phones at the office, so keeping them in bags conflicts with Passage 1.
n.2: The teacher never dismisses emergencies; Passage 1 describes a way to handle urgent messages.
n.3: Passage 1 says phones stay at the office until dismissal, so lunch use is not part of the policy.

R.q:
Passage 1
City council member Ortiz: Painted bike lanes do little when a delivery truck can park in them. Protected lanes, separated from traffic by curbs or posts, are the surest way to make cycling safe enough that families will try it. The city should build them on its three busiest streets.

Passage 2
City council member Bennett: Protected lanes cost about ten times as much per mile as paint. For the same money, we could add painted lanes across the city and lower the downtown speed limit to 20 miles per hour, which would protect cyclists on every street, not just three.

Which assumption do both council members share?
o: The city's budget cannot pay for any protected bike lanes.
Lower speed limits would reduce car traffic in the downtown area.
Protected lanes are the best choice for keeping cyclists safe.
Making streets safer for cyclists is a worthwhile goal for the city.
R.w: Ortiz and Bennett differ on the method, but both propose spending to protect cyclists. Neither questions the goal itself, so it is the assumption they share.

n.0: Bennett says protected lanes cost more, not that the city cannot afford any.
n.1: Bennett proposes lower speeds to protect cyclists, not to reduce traffic, and Ortiz does not mention speed.
n.2: This is Ortiz's position; Bennett argues that paint plus lower speeds would protect more cyclists.

R.q:
Sports drinks fill an entire aisle at most grocery stores, and sales in the United States topped $9 billion in 2023. A 20-ounce bottle of the leading brand contains 34 grams of sugar. In a 2021 survey, 58 percent of high school athletes said they drink sports drinks during practice. Registered dietitian Marcus Bell, who has advised college and professional teams for 20 years, put it plainly: "For anyone exercising less than an hour, sports drinks are a waste of money. Water is the smarter choice."

Which of the following statements from the article is an opinion?
o: A 20-ounce bottle of the leading brand contains 34 grams of sugar.
Sports drinks are a waste of money for anyone exercising less than an hour.
Fifty-eight percent of surveyed athletes said they drink sports drinks during practice.
Bell has advised college and professional teams for 20 years.
R.w: Calling a product "a waste of money" is a judgment of its value. Bell's long experience makes his view more credible, but an expert's judgment is still an opinion, not a fact.

n.0: Sugar content can be checked on the nutrition label, so it is a fact.
n.2: This reports the result of a survey. What the athletes said can be verified from the survey data, so it is a fact.
n.3: Bell's work history can be confirmed through the teams or his employment records, so it is a fact.

R.q:
Many older adults in Lakeview County miss medical appointments because they no longer drive and the nearest bus stop is more than a mile from the clinic. To fix this, the county launched a ride program last spring. First, a patient calls the clinic at least two days before the visit. Next, a dispatcher schedules a volunteer driver. Then the driver picks the patient up at home and waits during the appointment. In its first six months, the program provided 1,800 rides, and missed appointments fell by a third.

Which of the following best describes the overall organization of the passage?
o: cause and effect, because it explains why patients miss visits
compare and contrast, because it gives results before and after
chronological order, because it lists the steps a patient follows
problem and solution, because it presents a need and a response
R.w: The passage opens with a problem (missed appointments due to lack of transportation), describes the county's ride program as the fix, and reports its results. The ordered steps and the opening cause are parts of that larger problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: "Because" explains the problem in the first sentence, but most of the passage describes the program created to solve it.
n.1: A drop in missed appointments shows the solution worked; the passage does not set two subjects side by side.
n.2: "First," "next" and "then" order the steps of the solution, but they cover one section, not the passage as a whole.

R.q:
For a research methods class, Sofia reads an article in a peer-reviewed nursing journal. In it, the authors describe a study they conducted at three hospitals, comparing two methods of preventing pressure injuries in 400 patients. The article explains their methods, presents their data in tables, and discusses what their results mean. Sofia lists the article as a secondary source because it was published in a journal and includes the authors' analysis.

Is Sofia's classification correct?
o: No; it is a primary source because the authors report their own original study.
Yes; it is a secondary source because it appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.
Yes; it is a secondary source because it interprets data using statistics.
No; it is a tertiary source because journals are indexed in library databases.
R.w: A research article in which the authors present their own study and data is a primary source. Analysis of one's own results does not make it secondary; a review of other people's studies would be.

n.1: Publication in a journal does not decide the type; journals publish both primary studies and secondary reviews.
n.2: Researchers analyzing their own data are still reporting original work, so the article stays primary.
n.3: Being indexed in a database does not make an article tertiary; indexes are tertiary, the articles they list are not.

R.q:
Vitamin D is unusual among vitamins because the body can make it. When skin is exposed to the ultraviolet B (UVB) rays in sunlight, it produces a form of vitamin D that the liver and kidneys then activate. The amount of UVB reaching the ground depends on the angle of the sun. In winter, at places north of about 37 degrees latitude, the sun sits so low that little UVB reaches the ground, and the skin makes little vitamin D however long a person stays outside. Foods such as fatty fish, eggs, and fortified milk also supply the vitamin. Harborview lies at 42 degrees north latitude; Palmetto lies at 33 degrees north.

Based on the passage, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Residents of Harborview can make up for winter by spending more hours outdoors.
Winter sunlight gives Harborview residents less vitamin D than it gives Palmetto residents.
Residents of Harborview have lower vitamin D levels all year than residents of Palmetto.
Residents of Palmetto do not need vitamin D from food during the winter months.
R.w: Two details combine: north of about 37 degrees, winter sun produces little vitamin D in skin, and Harborview (42 degrees) is north of that line while Palmetto (33 degrees) is south of it.

n.0: This contradicts the passage: north of 37 degrees in winter, the skin makes little vitamin D however long a person stays outside.
n.2: The passage limits the latitude effect to winter and says food also supplies vitamin D, so year-round levels cannot be concluded.
n.3: The passage says Palmetto residents can make vitamin D from winter sun, but it does not say they need none from food.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The night before her TEAS exam, Aaliyah laid out her ID and admission ticket by the front door. She woke at six, an hour before her alarm, and reviewed her flashcards over breakfast. On the drive to the testing center, she realized she had left her ID by the door and turned back for it, arriving with ten minutes to spare. The Reading section felt fast; she finished it just as the timer ran out. During the break after the Math section, she ate a granola bar and texted her mother that the hardest part was over.

Which statement about the order of events is accurate?
o: Aaliyah texted her mother before she finished the Reading section.
Aaliyah laid out her ID after she woke on the morning of the exam.
Aaliyah reviewed her flashcards after she turned back for her ID.
Aaliyah finished the Math section before she texted her mother.
R.w: She texted her mother during the break, and the break came after the Math section. So the Math section was finished before the text.

n.0: Reversed: the text came during the break after Math, which followed the Reading section.
n.1: Reversed: she laid out her ID the night before the exam.
n.2: Reversed: she reviewed flashcards at breakfast, before the drive on which she turned back.

R.q:
Starting next month, Summit Medical Group will ask patients to complete their check-in forms online before they arrive. Patients who arrive without completing the form can fill it out on a tablet in the waiting room, which takes about 10 minutes. During a three-month pilot at one office, average check-in time at the front desk fell from 7 minutes to 2 minutes for patients who completed the form at home. About a third of the patients in the pilot arrived without completing it.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage?
o: Summit will remove the waiting-room tablets after next month because few patients use them.
Many patients will stop booking appointments with Summit because of the new form.
Patients who skip the online form will likely take longer to check in than those who complete it.
Average check-in time at each Summit office will likely fall to about 2 minutes per patient.
R.w: Patients who completed the form at home checked in in about 2 minutes, while those who arrive without it need about 10 minutes on a tablet. The passage supports a longer check-in for patients who skip the form.

n.0: About a third of pilot patients needed the tablet, so the passage suggests the tablets will be used, not removed.
n.1: Nothing in the passage suggests patients will leave; this prediction has no support.
n.3: Two minutes applied to patients who completed the form; with about a third arriving without it, the overall average would be higher.

R.q:
Read the description of the organizational chart.

Riverside Medical Center, Nursing Department
Chief Nursing Officer: Dr. Angela Brooks
Reporting directly to Dr. Brooks: Mark Ellis, Director of Inpatient Services; Sofia Ramirez, Director of Outpatient Services; Grace Kim, Director of Nursing Education
Reporting to Mark Ellis: Tom Nguyen, Nurse Manager, Medical-Surgical Unit; Leah Adams, Nurse Manager, Intensive Care Unit
Reporting to Sofia Ramirez: Ben Ortiz, Nurse Manager, Surgery Center; Ruth Hale, Clinic Coordinator
Reporting to Grace Kim: Jamal Price, Clinical Educator
Reporting to Leah Adams: ICU Day Charge Nurse; ICU Night Charge Nurse

According to the chart, to whom does the ICU night charge nurse's direct supervisor report?
o: Leah Adams
Sofia Ramirez
Dr. Angela Brooks
Mark Ellis
R.w: The ICU night charge nurse reports to Leah Adams (step 1). Leah Adams reports to Mark Ellis (step 2), so Mark Ellis is the answer.

n.0: Leah Adams is the charge nurse's direct supervisor; the question asks whom she reports to.
n.1: Sofia Ramirez oversees outpatient services, not the ICU.
n.2: Dr. Brooks is one level higher: Mark Ellis reports to her.

R.q:
Marisol, a nursing student, is preparing a teaching sheet for a patient who has just been prescribed a new blood thinner. She wants to list the foods and other medicines that can interact with it. Her options are the official prescribing information published with the drug, a health news website's article about the drug's approval, a popular health app's summary written by its staff, and a pharmacology textbook printed before the drug was approved.

Which source is best for this purpose?
o: The official prescribing information for the drug
The pharmacology textbook printed before approval
The health news article about the drug's approval
The health app's summary written by its staff
R.w: The official prescribing information lists the drug's known interactions in detail and is the authoritative, product-specific source.

n.1: A textbook printed before the drug was approved cannot include it.
n.2: A news article about approval gives a general story, not a complete list of interactions.
n.3: An app's staff summary is secondhand and may leave out details.

R.q:
The Brookside Health Fair drew about 600 visitors to the community center on Saturday. Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks, and a dentist handed out toothbrushes to children. Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring. Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line. Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.

Which sentence from the passage most clearly reveals the author's perspective?
o: Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks.
Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring.
Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.
Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line.
R.w: "Sadly" is the author's own reaction, and it shows concern that the fair fell short in an important area. The other sentences report events or quote someone else without the author adding a judgment.

n.0: This neutrally reports a service that was offered.
n.1: "Our best fair yet" is a judgment, but it is the organizers' view, which the author quotes. A view the author reports is not the author's own perspective.
n.2: This sentence supports the author's concern, but it reports a checkable outcome without any judgment word; it does not state the author's attitude as clearly as "Sadly" does.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Start with the number 4,729. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Swap the first digit and the last digit.
2. Add 1 to every even digit.
3. Remove the digit in the hundreds place.
4. Multiply the result by 2.
5. If the result is greater than 1,500, subtract 500 from it; otherwise, add 500 to it.

What is the final result?
R.w: Step 1: 9,724. Step 2 (2 becomes 3 and 4 becomes 5): 9,735. Step 3 removes the hundreds digit, 7: 935. Step 4: 935 x 2 = 1,870. Step 5: 1,870 is greater than 1,500, so subtract 500: 1,370.

n.1: Stops after step 4 and skips the conditional step.
n.2: Takes the wrong branch of step 5, adding 500 instead of subtracting it.
n.3: Removes the tens digit (3) instead of the hundreds digit, giving 975, then 1,950, then 1,450.

R.q:
Last school year, three children were struck by cars while walking to Garfield Elementary. All three accidents happened at the Elm Street and Fourth Avenue intersections, the only crossings near the school without an adult crossing guard. The school board should hire two more crossing guards before classes start in August. The cost, about $18,000 a year, is small compared with the medical bills from even one serious injury.

Which assumption links the author's evidence to the claim?
o: Crossing guards lower the chance that children are struck at intersections.
The number of children walking to Garfield will rise in the coming school year.
Garfield's guarded crossings carry less car traffic than Elm Street and Fourth Avenue.
Drivers near Garfield are less careful than drivers in other parts of town.
R.w: The evidence is that accidents happened at crossings without guards; the claim is that guards should be hired. The argument works only if guards actually make those crossings safer for children.

n.1: The argument rests on last year's accidents at unguarded crossings; it does not depend on more children walking.
n.2: Lighter traffic at the guarded crossings would be another explanation for where the accidents happened, so it would weaken the argument rather than link it.
n.3: The argument compares crossings with and without guards, not drivers in different parts of town.

R.q:
Podcast transcript, Dr. Lena Kim, sleep researcher: "During puberty, teenagers' internal clocks shift later, so many simply aren't sleepy until 11 p.m. or later. Asking a teenager to wake up at 6 is a bit like asking an adult to wake up at 4."

Newspaper article: A survey of 2,000 high school students in the state found that 70 percent slept less than eight hours on school nights. Students whose first class began at 7:30 a.m. averaged 6.8 hours of sleep.

Which statement is supported by both sources?
o: Teenagers' internal clocks shift later during the years of puberty.
Starting school at 9 a.m. would give teenagers two more hours of sleep.
Early school schedules can leave many teenagers short of sleep.
Seventy percent of high school students sleep less than eight hours.
R.w: Dr. Kim explains that early waking clashes with teenagers' late sleep timing, and the article's data show short sleep, especially with 7:30 a.m. starts. Both point to early schedules cutting teens' sleep.

n.0: This comes from the podcast only; the article does not discuss internal clocks.
n.1: Neither source measures the effect of a 9 a.m. start; this goes beyond both.
n.3: This comes from the article only; Dr. Kim gives no survey figures.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The Eastfield Library's summer reading challenge runs from June 10 to August 15. Readers of all ages may sign up at any branch or online. Children up to age 12 log minutes read; teens and adults log books finished. Every 300 minutes or every three books earns a ticket for the end-of-summer prize drawing, held August 22 at the main branch. Participants do not need to be present to win. Children who log 1,000 minutes also receive a free book of their choice, and teens who finish ten books earn a pass to the county pool. Last year, 2,140 people took part, up from 1,600 the year before.

Which of the following does the passage state? Select all that apply.
o: The prize drawing is held on August 22 at the main branch.
Teens and adults keep track of the number of books they finish.
Adults who finish ten books earn a pass to the county pool.
Participation grew by more than 1,000 people from the year before.
Prize winners must attend the drawing in order to collect a prize.
Children who log 1,000 minutes receive a free book of their choice.
R.w: The passage states that teens and adults log books finished, that children who log 1,000 minutes get a free book, and that the drawing is held August 22 at the main branch.

n.2: Wrong group: the pool pass is for teens who finish ten books, not adults.
n.3: Misreads the figures: participation rose from 1,600 to 2,140, an increase of 540 people.
n.4: Contradicted: participants do not need to be present to win.

R.q:
(1) The Eastside branch library should stay open until 9 p.m. on weeknights instead of closing at 6. (2) Many adults in our neighborhood work until 5:30 and cannot reach the branch before it closes. (3) When the branch tested evening hours last fall, it checked out 1,800 more items in two months. (4) Some board members say the extra hours would cost too much in staff pay. (5) However, the test was staffed by volunteers from the Friends of the Library, who have offered to continue. (6) Our neighbors deserve a library they can actually use.

Which sentence is a rebuttal?
o: Sentence 5
Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
R.w: Sentence 4 raises an objection (staff costs). Sentence 5, beginning with "However," answers that objection by noting volunteers covered the test and have offered to continue. A rebuttal is a response to a counterclaim.

n.1: Sentence 3 is evidence from the trial period supporting the claim.
n.2: Sentence 2 is a reason supporting the claim; it does not answer an objection.
n.3: Sentence 4 is the counterclaim itself, the objection that Sentence 5 rebuts.

R.q:
Two years ago, Cedar Ridge Hospital began letting its nurses choose either 8-hour or 12-hour shifts. In a recent staff survey, 70 percent of nurses on 12-hour shifts said they had more days available for family, compared with 35 percent of nurses on 8-hour shifts. However, 40 percent of nurses on 12-hour shifts said they felt very tired at the end of a shift, compared with 25 percent of those on 8-hour shifts. The rate at which nurses left the hospital was similar in both groups.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Most nurses at Cedar Ridge Hospital now prefer 12-hour shifts to 8-hour shifts.
Nurses on 8-hour shifts are less likely than others to leave the hospital.
Nurses on 12-hour shifts tend to trade more fatigue for more days with family.
Twelve-hour shifts lead to more patient care errors than 8-hour shifts.
R.w: Nurses on 12-hour shifts were twice as likely to report more family days (70% vs 35%) and also more likely to feel very tired (40% vs 25%), so the passage supports a trade-off.

n.0: The passage gives survey results within each group but not how many nurses chose each shift, so preference cannot be concluded.
n.1: This contradicts the passage, which says the rate of leaving was similar in both groups.
n.3: Patient errors are never mentioned; this relies on outside assumptions rather than the text.

R.q:
The county's proposal to close the Pine Street library branch, which opened in 1964, has drawn strong reactions. The county manager calls the branch "an expensive relic in the age of e-books." Several council members argue that the money would be better spent on road repairs. But the branch is the only place in the neighborhood with free internet access, and I see seniors there every day filling out benefit forms they cannot complete at home. Closing it would cut off people who have no other option. The county should find savings elsewhere.

Which statements from the passage express the author's own point of view? Select all that apply.
o: The Pine Street branch opened in 1964.
The proposal to close the branch has drawn strong reactions.
The money would be better spent on road repairs.
Closing it would cut off people who have no other option.
The branch is an expensive relic in the age of e-books.
The county should find savings elsewhere.
R.w: In the author's own sentences, the author judges that closing the branch would harm people with no alternative and concludes that the county should find savings elsewhere. These two statements express the author's position in favor of keeping the branch.

n.0: The opening date is a checkable background fact; it expresses no judgment about the proposal.
n.1: This is a neutral report that people have reacted strongly; it takes no side and does not state the author's own position.
n.2: This is the argument of several council members, which the author reports but does not share.
n.4: These are the county manager's words, quoted by the author in order to argue against them.

R.q:
Gabriela Ruiz is drafting a letter to her city council about drinking water. Her first draft begins, "The city's tap water is unsafe to drink." Her teacher points out that this sentence is an opinion as written. She suggests that Gabriela open with a fact that council members could verify for themselves, and then state her own view in a later sentence, so that her argument rests on evidence rather than on feeling.

Which revision follows her teacher's advice?
o: Experts agree that the city's tap water is probably unsafe for young children.
In a 2023 city test, water from 12 homes had lead above the federal action level.
The city's tap water is far too risky for families with babies and young children.
The city's tap water tastes worse than the bottled water sold in local stores.
R.w: A dated test with a stated number of homes and a federal standard can be checked against the city's test records, so it is a verifiable fact.

n.0: "Probably" signals a judgment, and claiming that experts agree does not make a judgment a fact. Expert opinion is still opinion.
n.2: "Far too risky" is a judgment about how much risk is acceptable, so the revision is still an opinion.
n.3: Taste is a matter of personal judgment; "tastes worse" cannot be proven.

R.q:
Letter to the student newspaper: The faculty senate is considering a policy that would let students retake one failed exam per course. This would be a mistake. If students know they can retake an exam, they will stop studying for first attempts. Soon nearly every exam will be taken twice, instructors will spend their time writing makeup tests instead of teaching, and within a few years employers will stop taking our degrees seriously.

Which fallacy does the letter contain?
o: Circular reasoning
Post hoc
Hasty generalization
Slippery slope
R.w: The writer claims one small policy will set off a chain of worsening results (no studying, every exam taken twice, worthless degrees) without evidence for each step. That is a slippery slope.

n.0: Circular reasoning restates its conclusion as its reason; the letter gives a (weak) chain of causes.
n.1: Post hoc claims a past event caused a later one because it came first; the letter predicts future consequences instead.
n.2: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from a few examples; the letter offers no examples.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Each year, thousands of people in the United States wait for a kidney transplant, and many will wait more than three years.

Consider Ray Delgado, a 52-year-old bus driver from Tucson. Ray spends four hours at a dialysis center three mornings a week. He has given up his route, his weekend softball league and the road trips he once took with his grandchildren. "I'm alive," he says, "but I'm waiting to live."

A single living donor can end that wait. Most healthy adults can donate a kidney and lead normal lives afterward, and the donor's medical costs are generally covered. Anyone curious about donating can contact a transplant center for a free screening.

What is the most likely purpose of the second paragraph?
o: To give a personal example that makes the long wait feel real to readers
To present an opposing view on whether to become a living donor
To suggest that bus drivers face a higher risk of kidney disease
To explain the medical steps involved in kidney dialysis treatment
R.w: The first paragraph states a statistic about long waits. The second turns that number into one person's life: the hours on dialysis, the activities he gave up and his own words. The detail humanizes the problem before the final paragraph asks readers to consider donating.

n.1: Ray's story supports the case for donation; no opposing view appears in the passage.
n.2: Ray's job is a personal detail; the passage makes no claim about bus drivers' risk.
n.3: The paragraph mentions how long Ray spends at dialysis but never explains the treatment's steps.

R.q:
Read the passage.

After Brookside Hospital placed hand-sanitizer dispensers outside every patient room on its surgical unit, managers tracked how often staff cleaned their hands. Before the change, observers saw staff clean their hands at about half of the moments when they should have. Six months later, the rate had risen to about three quarters. Over the same period, the number of infections patients picked up on the unit fell by about a fifth. During those six months, the hospital also hired two infection-prevention nurses, who ran training sessions on every unit.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Hand cleaning rose after the change, though the dispensers may not be the sole reason for it.
The dispensers probably did more than the nurses' training to raise hand cleaning.
Infections on the unit fell by about three quarters, likely because hand cleaning improved.
The infection-prevention nurses, rather than the dispensers, caused the drop in infections.
R.w: The rate of hand cleaning clearly rose (from about half to about three quarters), but the new nurses' training happened during the same six months. The evidence supports the rise while leaving the cause uncertain, which is what this option says.

n.1: Unsupported: the dispensers and the training began in the same six months, and the passage gives no way to compare their effects.
n.2: Misreads the figures: infections fell by about a fifth; about three quarters is the new hand-cleaning rate.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no way to separate the effect of the training from the effect of the dispensers.

R.q:
After her knee replacement, Mrs. Tran was ambulatory by the second day; that is, she could make it to the end of the hallway and back with a cane for support. The physical therapist recorded her distance each afternoon and expected her to manage the stairs before the end of the week.

As used in the passage, the word ambulatory most nearly means
o: free of pain.
in need of an ambulance.
ready to go home.
able to walk.
R.w: The phrase "that is" introduces a restatement: she could make it down the hallway and back with a cane. Ambulatory means able to walk.

n.0: The passage says nothing about pain; walking with a cane does not tell us whether she still hurts.
n.1: "Ambulance" looks and sounds similar, but the passage describes her moving on her own, not being transported.
n.2: Discharge is not mentioned, and the therapist still expects more progress this week, so "ready to go home" goes beyond the clue.

R.q:
Read the passage.

By the time the ambulance reached Mercy Hospital, Elena had already called her brother twice. She had found their father on the kitchen floor that morning, awake but unable to lift his right arm. Earlier, at breakfast, he had complained that his coffee tasted strange and that his words felt "thick." Elena, a first-year nursing student, remembered a lecture from the week before about the warning signs of a stroke, and she dialed 911 before helping him sit up. Now, in the waiting room, she wished she had paid closer attention when he slurred his words at breakfast.

Place the events in the order in which they occurred, starting with the earliest.
o: Elena finds her father on the kitchen floor
Elena's father complains that his coffee tastes strange
Elena dials 911
Elena attends a lecture on the warning signs of a stroke
The ambulance reaches Mercy Hospital
R.w: The passage opens near the end and looks back. The lecture was "the week before." Breakfast came "earlier" than finding him on the floor. Elena dialed 911 after finding him (before helping him sit up). The ambulance's arrival at the hospital is the latest event described before the waiting-room scene.

R.q:
Read the passage and the student's summary.

Passage: Community fridges are refrigerators placed on sidewalks or outside businesses where anyone can leave or take food at any hour. Many appeared in U.S. cities in 2020, when job losses left more families short on groceries. Most are run by volunteers, who clean them, check dates and post rules, and local bakeries and grocers often donate unsold food. Organizers say the fridges succeed because they ask no questions; people who feel embarrassed to visit a food pantry can take what they need without signing a form. Keeping the fridges clean and stocked, however, depends on a steady supply of volunteers.

Student's summary: (1) Community fridges are public refrigerators where anyone can leave or take food at any time. (2) Volunteers keep them clean, and stores donate unsold food. (3) Their no-questions approach is the best way to fight hunger in America. (4) Their success depends on a steady supply of volunteers.

Which sentence should be removed from the student's summary?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
R.w: A summary must be objective and add nothing new. The passage reports that organizers credit the no-questions approach for the fridges' success; it never claims this is the best way to fight hunger nationwide. Sentence 3 adds the student's own judgment.

n.0: Sentence 1 accurately restates the opening definition, which a summary needs.
n.2: Sentence 2 condenses the key point about how the fridges are run and supplied.
n.3: Sentence 4 restates the passage's closing point about the fridges' reliance on volunteers.

R.q:
Passage 1
From the hospital newsletter: In this year's staff survey, 60 percent of our nurses said they would recommend Lakeside General as a place to work. That result reflects the strong teamwork and pride our nursing staff bring to every shift.

Passage 2
From a nurses' union bulletin: The same survey means that 40 percent of nurses would not recommend Lakeside as a workplace. With one in five nurses leaving each year, management should treat this number as a warning, not a reason to celebrate.

The authors disagree mainly about
o: whether nurse morale affects the quality of patient care
what the survey result shows about nurses' morale
whether the survey was conducted by the hospital itself
how many nurses said they would recommend the hospital
R.w: Both accept the same figure (60 percent would recommend, so 40 percent would not). The newsletter reads it as a sign of pride; the union reads it as a warning. They disagree about interpretation.

n.0: Neither passage discusses patient care.
n.2: Neither passage raises who conducted the survey.
n.3: Both use the same survey figures, so they agree about the numbers.

R.q:
After 34 years at Riverside Hospital, Nurse Paulette Greene retired last Friday. Former students lined the hallway to thank her. Many said they still hear her voice when they check an IV line. She was famous for her candid feedback: if a student's technique was wrong, she said so plainly, then stayed until the student got it right. "She told me the truth when I needed it most," one former student said.

Which word could replace candid without changing the author's admiring tone?
o: tactless
honest
brutal
blunt
R.w: "Honest" keeps both the meaning (saying things plainly and truthfully) and the positive connotation that fits an admiring tribute.

n.0: "Tactless" means insensitive to others' feelings, a clearly negative connotation that clashes with the praise.
n.2: "Brutal" suggests harshness or cruelty, which contradicts the patient teacher who stayed until students succeeded.
n.3: "Blunt" shares the meaning of speaking plainly, but it suggests abruptness or lack of tact, which would add a critical edge to the tribute.

R.q:
In January, the Westfield Public Library began lending free home blood pressure monitors. The librarian says the program was designed to reach residents who do not see a doctor regularly. Borrowers may fill out an optional survey when they return a monitor.
Month | Monitor loans
January | 18
February | 31
March | 47
April | 52
Optional survey, January to April: 40 percent of borrowers who responded said they had not had their blood pressure checked in the past year.

Which conclusions are supported by the information above? Select all that apply.
o: Most borrowers had not had their blood pressure checked in the past year.
Some borrowers had gone more than a year without a blood pressure check.
Monitor loans increased every month from January through April.
Monitor loans will keep rising every month for the rest of the year.
Borrowers' blood pressure readings improved after they used the monitors.
The library made a total of 148 monitor loans from January through April.
R.w: Loans rose each month (18, 31, 47, 52) and total 148. The survey shows that 40 percent of respondents had gone a year without a check, so at least some borrowers had.

n.0: Forty percent of respondents is less than half, so "most" is not supported.
n.3: The data stop in April and growth slowed sharply (up 13, then 16, then only 5), so a rise every month is not supported.
n.4: Neither source reports any blood pressure readings or changes.

M.q: The table lists hours studied (x) and exam score (y) for seven students: (2, 61), (3, 66), (4, 70), (5, 52), (6, 79), (7, 83), (8, 88). When the data are graphed on a scatterplot, which point does not fit the overall trend?
M.w: Scores rise about 4 to 5 points per extra hour, so a student who studied 5 hours would be expected to score about 74. A score of 52 sits far below the pattern.

n.0: (8, 88) is the highest point, but it continues the upward trend.
n.1: (4, 70) is about 4 points above (3, 66), in line with the trend.
n.3: (2, 61) has the lowest x-value, and its score fits the rising pattern from the left.

M.q: A bottle contains 0.6 liter of sterile saline. A nurse pours out 3 doses of 85 milliliters each for wound care. How many milliliters of saline remain in the bottle? Enter your answer in milliliters.

tr.515: Subtracted one 85 mL dose instead of all three.
tr.5745: Converted 0.6 L to 6,000 mL (four places) before subtracting 255 mL.

M.w: Convert the bottle to milliliters: 0.6 L × 1,000 = 600 mL. Amount poured = 3 × 85 = 255 mL. Remaining = 600 - 255 = 345 mL.

M.q: The scale on a trail map is 2 centimeters to 0.5 kilometer. A hike measures 13 centimeters on the map. What is the actual length of the hike?
o: 3.25 kilometers
26 kilometers
52 kilometers
6.5 kilometers
M.w: Set up 2/0.5 = 13/d. Cross-multiply: 2d = 6.5, so d = 3.25 kilometers. (1 cm represents 0.25 km, and 13 × 0.25 = 3.25.)

n.1: This multiplies 13 by 2 and leaves out the 0.5 km.
n.2: This sets up the proportion upside down, multiplying 13 by 2 ÷ 0.5.
n.3: This multiplies 13 by 0.5 as if 1 cm represented 0.5 km; it is 2 cm that represents 0.5 km.

M.q: A newborn weighs 3,400 grams at birth, and the parents ask for the weight in pounds. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. What is the newborn's weight in pounds? Enter the number of pounds, rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.7480: Multiplied 3,400 g by 2.2 without first converting grams to kilograms.
tr.1.5: Divided 3.4 kg by 2.2; kilograms to pounds means multiplying.
tr.7.4: Truncated 7.48 instead of rounding; the hundredths digit 8 rounds the tenths digit up.

M.q: A pharmacy compares the active-ingredient fractions of five generic products. Place the values in order from least to greatest, starting with the least: 0.4, 38%, 7/20, 0.305, 3/8.
M.w: Convert each value to a decimal: 0.305; 7/20 = 0.35; 3/8 = 0.375; 38% = 0.38; 0.4 = 0.400. Least to greatest: 0.305 < 0.35 < 0.375 < 0.38 < 0.4. Adding zeros to compare (0.380 vs 0.375 vs 0.400) avoids the trap of thinking more digits means a bigger number.

M.q: Which value of n makes the equation 6n - 4(n - 2) = 30 true?
M.w: Distribute: 6n - 4n + 8 = 30. Combine like terms: 2n + 8 = 30. Subtract 8: 2n = 22. Divide by 2: n = 11. Check: 66 - 4(9) = 66 - 36 = 30.

n.0: This adds 6n and 4n instead of subtracting, giving 10n + 8 = 30.
n.2: This distributes the -4 to n only, giving 6n - 4n - 2 = 30, so 2n = 32.
n.3: Sign error: -4 × (-2) = +8, but this uses -8, giving 2n - 8 = 30.

M.q: A health class lists four pairs of variables that could be graphed on scatterplots. Which pair would most likely show a negative correlation?
o: Outdoor temperature and monthly heating cost
Household size and weekly grocery spending
A child's height and arm span
Hours worked and gross weekly pay
M.w: As outdoor temperature rises, less heating is needed, so heating cost tends to fall: one variable increases while the other decreases.

n.1: Larger households tend to spend more on groceries, a positive correlation.
n.2: Taller children tend to have longer arm spans, a positive correlation.
n.3: More hours worked brings more gross pay, a positive correlation.

M.q: Malik earns $17.50 per hour and worked 32 hours this week. 15% of his gross pay is withheld for taxes. From his take-home pay he pays $210 toward rent and $95 for groceries. How much of his take-home pay is left?

n.0: This subtracts the bills first and then takes 15% from what is left. Taxes are withheld from the full $560.
n.2: This is the take-home pay, an intermediate step; rent and groceries still have to be subtracted.
n.3: This subtracts rent and groceries from the gross pay of $560 and leaves out the 15% withheld for taxes.

M.q: Lena has $70 to spend on a phone case that costs $16 and some charging cables that cost $9.50 each. Ignoring tax, what is the greatest number of cables she can buy along with the case?
M.w: Write 16 + 9.50c ≤ 70. Subtract 16: 9.50c ≤ 54. Divide by 9.50: c ≤ 5.68. She can buy only whole cables, so the greatest number is 5 (5 × 9.50 = 47.50, total $63.50).

n.0: Sign error: this adds the $16 to $70 instead of subtracting it, giving 86 ÷ 9.50 ≈ 9.05.
n.1: This rounds 5.68 up. Six cables cost $57, and $57 + $16 = $73, which is over $70.
n.3: This divides the whole $70 by $9.50 and ignores the $16 case.

M.q: At the same time of day, a nurse who is 5.5 feet tall casts a shadow 4 feet long, and a flagpole outside the hospital casts a shadow 18 feet long. How tall is the flagpole?
o: 16.5 feet
13.09 feet
24.75 feet
19.5 feet
M.w: Height/shadow is the same for both: 5.5/4 = h/18. Cross-multiply: 4h = 99, so h = 24.75 feet.

n.0: This subtracts the 1.5-foot difference from the shadow length. Similar figures scale by multiplying.
n.1: This sets up the second ratio upside down, giving 4 × 18 ÷ 5.5.
n.3: This adds the 1.5-foot difference between the nurse's height and shadow. Similar figures scale by multiplying.

M.q: At lunch a patient is served a 480 mL nutritional shake and a 240 mL cup of juice. She drinks 300 mL of the shake and all of the juice. What percent of the total fluid served did she drink?
M.w: Total served: 480 + 240 = 720 mL. Total drunk: 300 + 240 = 540 mL. Percent = part ÷ whole × 100 = 540 ÷ 720 × 100 = 75%.

n.1: This is the shake alone, 300 ÷ 480. The juice she drank and the juice served both belong in the totals.
n.2: This is the percent of the fluid she left (180 ÷ 720), not the percent she drank.
n.3: This averages the two percents (62.5% and 100%). The containers hold different amounts, so combine the milliliters first: 540 ÷ 720.

M.q: An L-shaped room is formed from a 20-foot by 12-foot rectangle with a 6-foot by 5-foot closet cut out of one corner. The closet is not part of the room. What is the floor area of the L-shaped room?
o: 270 ft²
64 ft²
240 ft²
210 ft²
M.w: Full rectangle = 20 × 12 = 240 ft². Closet = 6 × 5 = 30 ft². Room = 240 - 30 = 210 ft².

n.0: This adds the closet area (30 ft²) instead of subtracting it.
n.1: 64 ft is the perimeter of the L-shaped room, not its area.
n.2: This is the full rectangle; the 30 ft² closet must be subtracted.

M.q: A nurse measures a healing incision as 3 5/8 inches long and must record the length as a decimal in the electronic chart. Which decimal should be recorded?
M.w: Convert the fraction part: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. Add the whole number: 3 + 0.625 = 3.625.

n.0: 0.375 is the decimal for 3/8, not 5/8.
n.1: This writes the digits 5 and 8 after the decimal point instead of dividing 5 by 8.
n.2: This divides 8 by 5 (1.6) instead of 5 by 8, then adds 3.

M.q: A bar graph compares patient satisfaction at two clinics: Clinic A 84% and Clinic B 88%. The vertical axis starts at 82%, so Clinic B's bar appears three times as tall as Clinic A's. Which statement most accurately describes the data?
o: B's rating is about 200% higher than A's
B's rating is about 3 times A's, as the bar heights show
The difference cannot be found, since the axis does not start at 0
B's rating is 4 percentage points higher than A's
M.w: Read the values, not the bar heights: 88% - 84% = 4 percentage points. The axis starting at 82% makes the bars 2 and 6 units tall, which exaggerates the gap.

n.0: Bar heights of 2 and 6 would suggest a 200% increase, but the actual values differ by 4 points (about 4.8%).
n.1: The bars look 3 times as tall only because the axis is truncated; 88% is not 3 times 84%.
n.2: The values can still be read from the scale; a truncated axis distorts the picture, not the numbers.

M.q: On a medical-surgical unit, the ratio of RNs to LPNs is 5:3. There are 40 nurses on the unit in total. How many of the nurses are LPNs?
M.w: Total parts = 5 + 3 = 8. Each part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 nurses. LPNs = 3 parts × 5 = 15 (and RNs = 25; 15 + 25 = 40).

n.1: This is the number of RNs (5/8 of 40), not LPNs.
n.2: This takes 3/5 of 40, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole. LPNs are 3 of every 8 nurses.
n.3: This divides 40 into 5 parts. The ratio has 5 + 3 = 8 parts, so each part is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 nurses.

M.q: A pediatric clinic paints a height line on the wall at exactly 1 meter. Use 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters. Which of the following heights are greater than 1 meter? Select all that apply.
o: 1.1 yards
39 inches
3 feet 3.5 inches
40 inches
3 feet 2 inches
1.08 yards
M.w: 1 m = 100 cm. 40 in × 2.54 = 101.6 cm; 1.1 yd = 39.6 in = 100.58 cm; 3 ft 3.5 in = 39.5 in = 100.33 cm. All three are over 100 cm. The others are 99.06 cm, 98.76 cm and 96.52 cm.

n.1: 39 × 2.54 = 99.06 cm, just under 100 cm.
n.4: 3 ft 2 in = 38 in, and 38 × 2.54 = 96.52 cm, under 100 cm.

M.q: After a 20% discount, a home blood pressure monitor costs $52. What was the original price of the monitor?
M.w: The sale price is 80% of the original: 0.80 × original = 52. Original = 52 ÷ 0.80 = $65. Check: 20% of 65 is 13, and 65 - 13 = 52.

n.0: This adds 20 dollars instead of reversing a 20% discount.
n.2: This adds 20% of $52 to $52. The 20% was taken from the original price, so divide by 0.80 instead.
n.3: This takes another 20% off $52 instead of finding the price before the discount.

M.q: A bar graph of hospital admissions has a vertical axis that starts at 900. The 2024 bar shows 950 admissions and the 2025 bar shows 1,100 admissions, so the 2025 bar looks 4 times as tall. By what percent did admissions actually increase from 2024 to 2025? Round to the nearest tenth and enter the number only.

tr.150: the number of extra admissions, not the percent
tr.300: the visual increase in bar height (50 to 200)

M.w: Percent increase = (new - original) / original x 100 = (1,100 - 950) / 950 x 100 = 150 / 950 x 100 = 15.79%, about 15.8%. The truncated axis makes the bars 50 and 200 units tall, which suggests a 300% increase.

M.q: Each of the 15 employees at a pharmacy receives a raise of $2.00 per hour. Before the raise, the hourly wages had a mean of $18.40, a median of $17.75, and a range of $9.50. Which describes the wages after the raise?
o: Mean $20.40, median $19.75, range $11.50
Mean $20.40, median $19.75, range $9.50
Mean $18.53, median $19.75, range $9.50
Mean $20.40, median $17.75, range $9.50
M.w: Adding the same amount to every value adds it to the mean and the median, but the gap between the highest and lowest wage does not change. Mean 18.40 + 2 = 20.40; median 17.75 + 2 = 19.75; range stays 9.50.

n.0: The range does not change: the highest and lowest wages both rise by $2.
n.2: Each employee gets $2, so the mean rises by $2, not by 2 / 15.
n.3: The middle wage also rises by $2, so the median becomes $19.75.

M.q: The roof truss of a house is an isosceles triangle. The angle at the peak, between the two equal sloping sides, measures 112°. What is the measure of each of the two base angles of the truss?
M.w: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal. (180 - 112) ÷ 2 = 68 ÷ 2 = 34°.

n.0: This uses 360°, the angle sum of a quadrilateral, instead of 180°.
n.1: 68° is both base angles together (180 - 112); divide by 2.
n.3: This halves the peak angle; the base angles share what is left of 180°.

M.q: Two clinics both have a mean wait time of 20 minutes. The standard deviation of the wait times is 3 minutes at Clinic A and 9 minutes at Clinic B. Which statement is correct?
o: Clinic B's wait times are more spread out around 20 minutes
Clinic B's patients wait longer on average than Clinic A's
Clinic A sees more patients, so its wait times vary less
Clinic A's median wait time is greater than Clinic B's
M.w: Standard deviation measures spread: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean. A larger SD (9 vs 3) means Clinic B's waits vary more around the shared mean of 20.

n.1: Both clinics have the same mean of 20 minutes; SD describes spread, not the average.
n.2: SD does not depend on the number of patients; nothing in the data gives patient counts.
n.3: Standard deviation gives no information about which median is larger.

M.q: A caterer charges a $150 setup fee plus $18.50 per guest for a nursing school graduation party. Which statements about the cost are true? Select all that apply.
o: A budget of $1,000 covers at most 46 guests.
Doubling the guests from 40 to 80 doubles the total cost.
A bill of $1,075 corresponds to 50 guests.
The cost for 40 guests is $890.
The cost for 60 guests is $1,110.

n.0: (1,000 - 150) ÷ 18.50 = 45.9, so the budget covers at most 45 guests; 46 guests would cost $1,001.
n.1: 80 guests cost 150 + 1,480 = $1,630, not 2 × 890 = $1,780. The $150 fee is charged once, so the cost is not directly proportional to the number of guests.
n.4: 18.50 × 60 = $1,110 leaves out the $150 setup fee; the total is $1,260.

M.q: A nurse researcher studies whether patients' fasting blood glucose levels are affected by the number of steps they walk each day. Every patient wears the same model of step counter for 30 days, and glucose is always checked at 7 a.m. Which is the dependent variable?
o: Fasting blood glucose level
Number of steps walked each day
Time of day glucose is checked
Model of step counter worn
M.w: The dependent variable is the measured outcome that may respond to the change. The study asks whether glucose is affected by daily steps, so fasting glucose level depends on the number of steps walked.

n.1: Daily steps is the independent variable: it is the factor whose effect on glucose is being tested, even though it is named second.
n.2: Checking glucose at 7 a.m. for every patient holds this factor constant, which makes it a controlled variable.
n.3: Every patient wears the same model, so it is held constant: a controlled variable, not the measured outcome.

M.q: A dosage calculation gives a volume of 3.96 mL, and the syringe being used is marked in tenths of a milliliter. What is 3.96 rounded to the nearest tenth? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.3.1: Rounded the 9 up to 10 but did not carry the 1 into the ones place.

M.w: The tenths digit is 9. The hundredths digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so the 9 rounds up to 10, carrying 1 into the ones place: 3.96 → 4.0 mL (entered as 4).

M.q: A science student must simplify (8 × 10⁵) ÷ (2 × 10⁻²) and give the result in scientific notation. Which is the result?
M.w: Divide the coefficients: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Subtract the exponents: 5 - (-2) = 7. Result: 4 × 10⁷.

n.0: 4 × 10⁻¹⁰ multiplies the exponents (5 × -2).
n.2: 1.6 × 10⁴ multiplies the coefficients (8 × 2 = 16) while adding the exponents.
n.3: 4 × 10³ computes 5 + (-2) = 3; dividing powers of 10 means subtracting, and 5 - (-2) = 7.

M.q: A patient in a weight-management program weighed 182 pounds at week 2 and 173 pounds at week 6. What was the average rate of change in the patient's weight over this period?
o: -2.25 pounds per week
-0.44 pounds per week
-4.5 pounds per week
-1.5 pounds per week
M.w: Rate of change = change in weight ÷ change in time = (173 - 182) ÷ (6 - 2) = -9 ÷ 4 = -2.25 pounds per week.

n.1: This divides the weeks by the pounds (4 ÷ 9), which inverts the rate.
n.2: This divides the 9-pound change by 2, the starting week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.
n.3: This divides the 9-pound change by 6, the week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.

M.q: Five containers are being compared for a supply room. Use 3.14 for pi and 1 milliliter = 1 cubic centimeter. Place the containers in order from least volume to greatest volume, starting with the least.
o: A bottle that holds 0.95 L
A cube with 10 cm edges
A jug that holds 1,020 mL
A box 8 cm by 12 cm by 11 cm
A cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 12 cm
M.w: Convert each to cubic centimeters: cylinder = 3.14 × 5² × 12 = 942; bottle = 0.95 L = 950 mL = 950; cube = 10³ = 1,000; jug = 1,020; box = 8 × 12 × 11 = 1,056. Least to greatest: 942, 950, 1,000, 1,020, 1,056.

M.q: A school nurse surveys 270 students about how they get to school and plans a pie chart of the results: walk 45, bus 81, car 126, bike 18. What central angle should the bus sector have?
M.w: Bus fraction: 81 / 270 = 0.3. Central angle = 0.3 x 360° = 108°.

n.0: 126 / 270 x 360° = 168° is the car sector.
n.1: 81 is the number of bus riders, not degrees.
n.3: 30 is the percent (30%); as a decimal it must be multiplied by 360°.

M.q: A regional hospital system reported serving 248,513 patients last year. What is this number rounded to the nearest ten thousand?
M.w: The ten-thousands digit is 4 (in 248,513). The digit to its right is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up: 250,000.

n.0: 200,000 is rounded to the nearest hundred thousand.
n.1: 249,000 is rounded to the nearest thousand.
n.3: 240,000 truncates; the thousands digit 8 means rounding up.

M.q: On a math placement worksheet, a student must evaluate the expression 18 - 6 ÷ 3 × 2 + 4. What is its value?
M.w: Multiplication and division have equal rank, so work left to right: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, then 2 × 2 = 4. Then add and subtract left to right: 18 - 4 = 14, and 14 + 4 = 18.

n.0: 12 works strictly left to right from the start (18 - 6 first), ignoring that division and multiplication come before subtraction.
n.1: 21 multiplies 3 × 2 before dividing (6 ÷ 6 = 1); division comes first here because it is on the left.
n.2: 10 adds 4 + 4 before subtracting; addition and subtraction are done left to right.

M.q: Jordan earns $2,850 per month after taxes. Each month he pays $1,140 in rent, spends 1/6 of his after-tax income on food and puts $300 into savings. How much money does he have left each month?

n.0: $1,235 leaves out the $300 put into savings.
n.1: $1,410 leaves out the food spending.
n.2: $1,125 takes 1/6 of the money left after rent ($285) instead of 1/6 of his income.

M.q: Solve for x: x/6 + 4 = 11.
M.w: Subtract 4 from both sides: x/6 = 7. Multiply both sides by 6: x = 42. Check: 42/6 + 4 = 7 + 4 = 11.

n.0: Sign error: 4 was added to 11 instead of subtracted, giving x/6 = 15.
n.1: This divides by 6 instead of multiplying. To undo x/6, multiply both sides by 6.
n.3: This multiplies 11 by 6 but not the 4. Multiplying every term by 6 gives x + 24 = 66, so x = 42.

M.q: A physical therapist records that a patient's forward reach improved by 2 3/8 inches. Write this length as an exact decimal. Enter the number of inches only.

tr.0.375: Gave only the fraction part and dropped the 2 whole inches.

M.w: Divide the fraction part: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Add the whole number: 2 + 0.375 = 2.375 inches.

M.q: A sign is shaped like a parallelogram with a base of 2.5 meters and slanted sides of 1.3 meters. The perpendicular height between the two bases is 1.2 meters. What is the area of one face of the sign?
o: 3 m²
7.6 m²
1.5 m²
M.w: A = base × perpendicular height = 2.5 × 1.2 = 3 m².

n.0: This multiplies the base by the slanted side; the height must be perpendicular to the base.
n.2: 7.6 m is the perimeter, 2 × (2.5 + 1.3), not the area.
n.3: This takes half of base × height, which is the triangle formula.

M.q: On a number line, point Q is located exactly halfway between -1/2 and 3/4. What is the value of point Q?
M.w: The midpoint is the average: (-1/2 + 3/4) ÷ 2 = (-2/4 + 3/4) ÷ 2 = 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8. Check: from -1/2 up 5/8 gives 1/8, and from 1/8 up 5/8 gives 3/4.

n.0: 1/4 is the sum -1/2 + 3/4; it still needs to be divided by 2.
n.2: 5/8 is half of the distance between the points (1 1/4 ÷ 2), not the location of the midpoint.
n.3: -1/8 has the wrong sign; -2/4 + 3/4 is positive.

M.q: A scatterplot shows the hours of sleep the night before (x) and reaction time on a driving test, in milliseconds (y), for 25 adults. The points fall close to a straight line that slopes downward from left to right. Which best describes the relationship?
o: No correlation
Strong positive correlation
Weak negative correlation
Strong negative correlation
M.w: A downward slope from left to right means that as x increases, y tends to decrease: a negative correlation. Points close to a line make it strong.

n.0: No correlation is a cloud with no direction; these points follow a clear line.
n.1: A positive correlation rises from left to right; this pattern falls.
n.2: A weak correlation has widely scattered points; these fall close to the line.

M.q: The ordered data set 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 20 has a median of 9.5. A seventh value, 9, is added to the data set. What is the new median?
M.w: New ordered set: 3, 5, 8, 9, 11, 14, 20. With 7 values, the median is the 4th value, 9.

n.1: 9.5 was the median before the new value was added.
n.2: 70 / 7 = 10 is the new mean.
n.3: (8 + 9) / 2 = 8.5 averages two values, but an odd count has a single middle value.
